beats.intro: Chapter three. [[sub]]Probability gives us a language for uncertainty, and the rules to combine uncertain events.
beats.basics: [[a]]An outcome is one possible result, and an event is a set of outcomes. Probability is a number that says how likely an event is. [[rules]]It follows two rules. Every probability is between zero and one. And for events that are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, the probabilities add up to one. [[bar]]Say a stock can end the year up, flat, or down, with probabilities forty-five, fifteen, and forty percent. They cover every possibility, and the total is one hundred percent. [[emp]]Where do the numbers come from? Empirical probability comes from observed frequencies. [[subj]]Subjective probability comes from judgment. [[apr]]A priori probability comes from logic, like a fair die.
beats.odds: [[a]]Odds restate probability. Suppose an event has probability one in four. [[sq]]One of four equal chances is the event. [[for]]The odds for the event are the probability divided by one minus the probability: point two five over point seven five, which is one to three. [[against]]The odds against are the reverse: three to one. [[back]]To go back, odds of a to b give a probability of a divided by a plus b.
beats.conditional: [[a]]Here are one hundred stocks. Fifty are in the technology sector. Call that event A. [[b]]Forty rose this year: event B. [[ab]]Thirty are both. That is the joint probability, point three. [[cond]]Now suppose we know the stock rose. We look only at those forty. Thirty of them are technology stocks. [[eq]]So the conditional probability of A given B is the joint probability, point three, divided by the probability of B, point four: point seven five.
beats.rules: [[mult]]Rearranging gives the multiplication rule: the joint probability is the conditional probability times the probability of B. Point seven five times point four is point three. [[add]]The addition rule finds the probability of A or B. Add the two probabilities, then subtract the overlap, which was counted twice. Point five plus point four minus point three is point six.
beats.q2: Quick check. Use the addition rule.
beats.independent: [[a]]Two events are independent if knowing one tells us nothing about the other. [[grid]]Here A is the left half of the square, and B is the top four tenths. [[ov]]The overlap is twenty cells: point two. [[test]]That equals point five times point four. And the conditional probability of A given B is still point five. [[note]]For independent events, the joint probability is simply the product. Our earlier stocks were not independent: point seven five is not point five.
beats.total: [[a]]The total probability rule finds an unconditional probability from scenarios. Suppose the market is up with probability point six, or down with probability point four. [[s1]]If it is up, our stock rises with probability point seven. [[s2]]If it is down, only point two. [[sum]]Weight each branch by its scenario probability and add: point six times point seven, plus point four times point two, is point four two plus point oh eight: point five.
beats.counting: [[a]]Counting problems ask how many ways something can happen. [[mult]]The multiplication rule: if one task can be done in two ways and another in three, together there are six ways. [[fact]]Ordering all n items gives n factorial. Three analysts can be ranked in three times two times one: six orders. [[five]]And five funds can be ordered one hundred twenty ways.
beats.combos: [[a]]Now choose two items from four: A, B, C, D. [[comb]]When order does not matter, these are combinations: six of them. [[perm]]When order matters, each pair can be listed two ways: twelve permutations. [[fc]]The combination formula is n factorial over r factorial times n minus r factorial. [[fp]]The permutation formula leaves out the r factorial in the denominator.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Probabilities lie between zero and one. Over exclusive, exhaustive events they sum to one. Odds are P over one minus P. [[w2]]The conditional, multiplication and addition rules link joint and single probabilities. [[w3]]Independent events multiply, and total probability weights the scenarios. [[w4]]To count, use factorials, combinations when order is ignored, and permutations when it matters. [[end]]Now try the chapter practice.
beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of chapter three.
